validated_results.title: The association between plant protein intake and cancer risk: a prospective cohort study.
validated_results.reason: Prospective UK Biobank cohort reporting an adjusted hazard ratio for incident renal cancer comparing highest versus lowest quartile of dietary plant protein intake.

extraction.comparison_type: highest vs lowest quartile of plant protein intake
extraction.timing: recruited from 2006 and followed until 2023; median follow-up 11.2 years

sample_size.excerpt: This prospective cohort study included 192,428 participants from the UK Biobank, recruited from 2006 and followed until 2023.

effect_size.excerpt: Compared to participants in the lowest quartile of plant protein intake, those in the highest quartile had HRs for overall cancer, lung cancer, renal cancer, and colorectal cancer of 0.91 (95% CI = 0.88-0.95, P < 0.001), 0.86 (95% CI = 0.73-1.00, P = 0.048), 0.69 (95% CI = 0.55-0.87, P = 0.002), and 0.89 (95% CI = 0.79-1.00, P = 0.046), respectively. Furthermore, each 10% increase in the ratio of plant protein to total daily protein was associated with a 3% lower overall cancer risk (HR = 0.97, 95% CI = 0.95-0.98, P < 0.001).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Compared to participants in the lowest quartile of plant protein intake, those in the highest quartile had HRs for overall cancer, lung cancer, renal cancer, and colorectal cancer of 0.91 (95% CI = 0.88-0.95, P < 0.001), 0.86 (95% CI = 0.73-1.00, P = 0.048), 0.69 (95% CI = 0.55-0.87, P = 0.002), and 0.89 (95% CI = 0.79-1.00, P = 0.046), respectively.

gender.excerpt: Subgroup analyses suggested that the negative association was more pronounced in male.
